Set your torso and let your working arm hang with the shoulder blade relaxed forward.
Set a stable base before you begin pulling.

Draw the load to your lower ribs and squeeze your shoulder blade back.
Lower under control until your arm is straight and the shoulder blade reaches forward.

Lead with your elbow, not your hand.
Draw the load toward your belt line rather than your chest.

Pull with your back and squeeze your shoulder blades together, not just your arms.

Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower under control until your arms are straight.

Set your back flat and take a breath into your belly before you pull.

Stand up by driving your hips forward until you are tall.

Keep the load in contact with your legs from start to finish.

Set your feet and create full-body tension before you begin.

Press back to a full lockout.

Drive your shoulder blades back and down and hold that position.

Think about squeezing your chest to drive the movement, not just pushing with your arms.
Tuck your elbows to about 45 degrees from your torso.
Drive your shoulder blades back and down and hold that position.

Descend until your thighs reach at least parallel to the floor.
Drive through the middle of your foot to stand back up.

Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.

Squeeze your glutes and take a breath to keep your ribs down.

Lower under control back to shoulder height.

Squeeze your glutes to stop your lower back from arching.

Lower under control into a full stretch at the bottom.

Load your hips and take a breath before the explosive rep.
executionSteps: Be explosive on the way up, moving the load or your body as fast as possible.
Absorb the landing or return softly through your hips and knees.
Reset to a stable, balanced position before the next rep.
coachingTips: Be explosive on the way up and controlled on the way down.
Land softly on your mid-foot, absorbing through your hips and knees.
Reset fully between reps rather than rushing the next one.
Keep a firm grip and let your forearms do the work.
commonMistakes: Landing stiff-legged with a hard, loud impact.
Rushing reps and losing power output.
Letting the knees collapse inward on landing.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Landing stiff-legged with a hard, loud impact.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A stiff landing wastes the force your legs should be absorbing.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Land quietly and let your hips and knees bend to absorb the force.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rushing reps and losing power output.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Rushed reps are less explosive, and power is the whole point of the movement.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Take a full reset between reps so each one is maximally explosive.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the knees collapse inward on landing.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A collapsed-knee landing is a weak position to absorb force.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Land with your knees tracking over your toes and your hips back.

breathingGuidance: Take a breath and brace before each rep, then exhale on the effort.
tempoGuidance: Explode on the effort; land and reset under full control.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Complete the full jump, throw or drive, then reset before the next rep. Take the forearms through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Be explosive on the way up and controlled on the way down.
Keep a firm grip and let your forearms do the work.
Land softly on your mid-foot, absorbing through your hips and knees.
Reset fully between reps rather than rushing the next one.
advancedCoachingNotes: Increase height, distance or load only while landings stay quiet and controlled.
beginnerNotes: Start with lower height or lighter load and step down between reps.
equipmentSetup: Anchor the rope securely and take a stable, athletic stance with tension in the line.
safetyNotes: Reduce the load if you lose control of the movement.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain.
When you fatigue, step down rather than jumping down between reps.
difficultyConsiderations: The Battle Rope Circles is a battle-rope movement. The rope loads your effort continuously, so keep the waves going at a steady pace. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you can scale the effort and load to your level, and it rewards practising the technique.

whyItMatters: The Bayesian Curl builds strength and size in your biceps. As an isolation movement, it targets those muscles directly to build size and balance.
setupInstructions: Set the pulley to the right height, attach the handle, and step back to remove the slack before your first rep.
Set a tall torso with your upper arms pinned against your sides.
Start with your arms straight and the load under control.
executionSteps: Bend your elbows and curl the load up while keeping your upper arms still.
Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower under control until your arms are straight.
coachingTips: Keep your elbows pinned to your sides throughout.
Turn your pinky slightly up at the top to finish the squeeze.
Lower all the way until your arm is straight each rep.
Keep the tension on your biceps and stop your elbows from drifting forward.
Keep steady tension on the cable through the whole range, including the return.
commonMistakes: Swinging the torso to start the load moving.
Letting the elbows drift forward to lift the load higher.
Cutting the lower-half of the range short.
Letting the cable yank your arm back at the end of the rep.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Swinging the torso to start the load moving.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A torso swing starts the curl with momentum instead of your biceps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Stand tall and keep your upper arms fixed against your sides.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward to lift the load higher.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Moving the elbows turns a curl into a partial front raise and takes tension off your biceps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your elbows under your shoulders and stop the curl where your upper arm wants to move.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the lower-half of the range short.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Skipping the bottom half leaves strength and size on the table.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Straighten your arm fully at the bottom of each rep.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the cable yank your arm back at the end of the rep.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Giving in to the cable skips the lowering phase, cutting the work in half.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Control the return against the cable tension rather than giving in to it.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you curl up, breathe in as you lower.
tempoGuidance: Curl with control and lower for about two counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Move from a fully straight arm to a hard squeeze at the top. Take the biceps through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Keep your elbows pinned to your sides throughout.
Keep the tension on your biceps and stop your elbows from drifting forward.
Keep steady tension on the cable through the whole range, including the return.
Turn your pinky slightly up at the top to finish the squeeze.
Lower all the way until your arm is straight each rep.
advancedCoachingNotes: Slow the lowering phase to three counts to add time under tension.
beginnerNotes: Pick a load you can lift without swinging your body.
equipmentSetup: Set the pulley to the right height, attach the handle, and step back to remove the slack before your first rep.
difficultyConsiderations: The Bayesian Curl is an isolation cable movement. The cable holds constant tension on the muscle through the whole range, including the return. Your working limb moves freely, so keep the joint you are training under control. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because the cable is stable and easy to control, and it works one joint, so it is simpler to learn.

whyItMatters: The Bear Crawl builds your aerobic base, work capacity and conditioning.
setupInstructions: Set your effort to a pace you can sustain for the planned duration.
Settle into a rhythm before pushing the pace.
executionSteps: Hold a steady, repeatable rhythm for the working duration.
Keep your breathing matched to your pace throughout.
Adjust your effort so the last minute feels as controlled as the first.
coachingTips: Settle into a cadence you can hold for the full effort.
Breathe rhythmically and in time with your pace.
Build the pace gradually rather than starting too hard.
Keep your hips low and move your opposite hand and foot together.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
commonMistakes: Starting too fast and fading in the second half.
Tensing the shoulders and upper body while working.
Letting the effort drift down whenever your attention wanders.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Starting too fast and fading in the second half.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A fast start you cannot hold means the back half of the effort suffers.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Open at a pace you could hold to the end, then build.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Tensing the shoulders and upper body while working.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Tension up top wastes energy that should go into your legs and lungs.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Relax your hands, shoulders and face so the effort stays in your legs and lungs.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the effort drift down whenever your attention wanders.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Coasting drops the training effect for that stretch of the effort.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Check your pace regularly and hold it steady to the end.

breathingGuidance: Breathe in a steady rhythm matched to your cadence.
tempoGuidance: Hold a sustainable, repeatable pace for the target duration.
cueHierarchy: Settle into a cadence you can hold for the full effort.
Keep your hips low and move your opposite hand and foot together.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
Breathe rhythmically and in time with your pace.
Build the pace gradually rather than starting too hard.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add pace changes or intervals to raise the training stimulus.
beginnerNotes: Use intervals of easier effort to build duration over time.
difficultyConsiderations: The Bear Crawl is a bodyweight movement. You move and stabilise your own bodyweight, so change leverage to progress rather than adding weight. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you manage only your own bodyweight.

progressionGuidance.regressionReason: Drop back to Wall Walk to groove the movement before you add load or complexity.

whyItMatters: The Behind-the-Back Lateral Raise builds strength and size in your lateral deltoids. As an isolation movement, it targets those muscles directly to build size and balance.
setupInstructions: Set the pulley to the right height, attach the handle, and step back to remove the slack before your first rep.
Set a tall torso with a slight bend in your elbows.
Start with the load under control at your sides or front.
executionSteps: Lead with your elbows and raise the load to shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower the load under control to the start.
coachingTips: Lead with your elbow and stop around shoulder height.
Lead with your elbows and stop at shoulder height.
Keep a soft, fixed bend in your elbows throughout.
Lower under control rather than dropping the load.
Lead with your elbow and feel the side of your shoulder do the work.
commonMistakes: Swinging the weight up with a hip drive.
Swinging the load up with the torso.
Raising the load well above shoulder height and shrugging.
Letting the wrists roll or drop under the load.
Letting the cable yank your arm back at the end of the rep.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Swinging the weight up with a hip drive.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Slow it down and let the shoulder raise the weight on its own.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Swinging the load up with the torso.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Body swing does the lifting, so your shoulders get little out of it.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your torso still and raise the load with your shoulders, not momentum.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Raising the load well above shoulder height and shrugging.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Going too high brings your traps in and takes the work off the muscle you want.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Stop at shoulder height and keep your traps relaxed.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the wrists roll or drop under the load.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Bent wrists leak force and move the effort away from the muscle you want.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your wrists flat and level with your forearms throughout.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the cable yank your arm back at the end of the rep.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Giving in to the cable skips the lowering phase, cutting the work in half.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Control the return against the cable tension rather than giving in to it.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you raise, breathe in as you lower.
tempoGuidance: Raise with control and lower for about two counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Raise to shoulder height and lower to a light stretch at the start. Take the lateral deltoids through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Lead with your elbow and stop around shoulder height.
Lead with your elbows and stop at shoulder height.
Lead with your elbow and feel the side of your shoulder do the work.
Keep steady tension on the cable through the whole range, including the return.
Keep a soft, fixed bend in your elbows throughout.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add a pause at shoulder height before lowering.
beginnerNotes: Use a light load and stop the moment your form breaks down.
equipmentSetup: Set the pulley to the right height, attach the handle, and step back to remove the slack before your first rep.
difficultyConsiderations: The Behind-the-Back Lateral Raise is an isolation cable movement. The cable holds constant tension on the muscle through the whole range, including the return. Your working limb moves freely, so keep the joint you are training under control. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because the cable is stable and easy to control, and it works one joint, so it is simpler to learn.

progressionGuidance.regressionReason: Drop back to Machine Lateral Raise to groove the movement before you add load or complexity.
progressionGuidance.progressionReason: Move up to Dumbbell Lateral Raise once you can control this one for all your reps.

whyItMatters: The Belt Squat builds strength and size in your quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings and rectus abdominis. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Adjust the seat and any pads so the working joint lines up with the machine’s pivot, set the pin to your working weight, and keep contact with the support pad throughout.
Set your feet about shoulder-width with your toes turned out slightly.
Take a full breath into your belly and brace before you descend.
executionSteps: Break at the hips and knees together and lower under control.
Descend until your thighs reach at least parallel to the floor.
Drive through the middle of your foot to stand back up.
coachingTips: Keep the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Let your knees track in line with your toes.
Push your knees out as you descend into the bottom.
Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.
Follow the machine’s guided lever path smoothly and control the weight back to the stack.
commonMistakes: Letting the knees cave inward under load.
Rising hips-first so the load shifts forward onto your toes.
Cutting the depth short above parallel.
Letting the weight stack slam down at the bottom.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the knees cave inward under load.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Caved knees are a weaker position and rob power from the lift.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Push your knees out toward your little toes as you descend and stand.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rising hips-first so the load shifts forward onto your toes.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Hips shooting up first tips you forward and turns the squat into a good morning.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lead with your chest and drive your hips and shoulders up at the same rate.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the depth short above parallel.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shallow squat trains a fraction of the range and much less of your legs.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lower until your hip crease drops below the top of your knee.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the weight stack slam down at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A slammed stack means gravity did the lowering, not your muscles.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Control the return so the plates settle without banging.

breathingGuidance: Take a big breath at the top, hold it through the descent and drive, then exhale at the top.
tempoGuidance: Lower under control for about two counts, then stand with intent.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Aim for thighs at or below parallel while keeping your heels flat on the floor. Take the quadriceps through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Keep the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.
Follow the machine’s guided lever path smoothly and control the weight back to the stack.
Let your knees track in line with your toes.
Push your knees out as you descend into the bottom.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add a pause in the bottom position to build strength out of the hole.
beginnerNotes: Start with a box or bench behind you to learn consistent depth.
equipmentSetup: Adjust the seat and any pads so the working joint lines up with the machine’s pivot, set the pin to your working weight, and keep contact with the support pad throughout.
difficultyConsiderations: The Belt Squat is a compound machine movement. Because the machine guides the path, put your attention on driving with the target muscle. Your hands or feet stay planted, so you move your body against the resistance. It suits newer athletes and is a good place to build the pattern.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Beginner because the machine guides the path, so there is little balance to manage, and it coordinates several joints at once.

progressionGuidance.progressionReason: Move up to Cable Belt Squat once you can control this one for all your reps.

whyItMatters: The Bench Dip builds strength and size in your chest, front deltoids and triceps. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Support your weight on the handles or bars with your arms straight and your shoulders pulled down.
Set a slight forward lean and brace before you lower.
executionSteps: Lower under control by bending your elbows until your upper arms are about parallel to the floor.
Keep your elbows tracking back rather than flaring wide.
Press back up until your arms are straight.
coachingTips: Lower until your upper arms reach about parallel to the floor.
Keep your elbows tracking back over your wrists, not flaring out.
Lean your torso forward slightly to bias the chest, or stay upright to bias the triceps.
Think about squeezing your chest to drive the movement, not just pushing with your arms.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
commonMistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears at the bottom.
Only dipping a few inches instead of reaching depth.
Letting the elbows flare wide as you press.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Shrugged shoulders put your shoulder in a weaker, more exposed position at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your shoulders pulled down and away from your ears throughout.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Only dipping a few inches instead of reaching depth.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shallow dip trains a small slice of the range and much less of your chest and triceps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lower until your upper arms are about parallel to the floor.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the elbows flare wide as you press.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Wide elbows put your shoulders in a weaker position to press from.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your elbows tracking back over your wrists.

breathingGuidance: Breathe in as you lower, exhale as you press up.
tempoGuidance: Lower for about two counts, then press up with intent.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Lower until your upper arms are about parallel, then press to straight arms. Take the chest through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Lower until your upper arms reach about parallel to the floor.
Think about squeezing your chest to drive the movement, not just pushing with your arms.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
Keep your elbows tracking back over your wrists, not flaring out.
Lean your torso forward slightly to bias the chest, or stay upright to bias the triceps.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add a pause at the bottom or progress the difficulty once you own full-depth reps.
beginnerNotes: Use band or machine assistance, or keep the range shallow, until you can control full-depth reps.
difficultyConsiderations: The Bench Dip is a compound bodyweight movement. You move and stabilise your own bodyweight, so change leverage to progress rather than adding weight. Your hands or feet stay planted, so you move your body against the resistance. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you manage only your own bodyweight, and it coordinates several joints at once.

whyItMatters: The Bicycle Crunch builds strength and size in your obliques. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Lie on your back with your feet flat and your lower back in a neutral position.
Set your position and take the slack out of your midsection before you begin.
Start each rep from a controlled, stable position.
executionSteps: Move slowly and deliberately through the working range.
Pause briefly where your midsection is working hardest.
Control the return rather than dropping quickly at the end.
Curl your ribs toward your hips, lifting one vertebra at a time.
coachingTips: Move your ribs toward your pelvis rather than yanking on your neck.
Move under control — no yanking or rushing the reps.
Curl your ribs toward your hips rather than pulling with your neck.
Keep the tension on your midsection, not your hip flexors or lower back.
Rotate or bend from your waist and feel the side of your trunk work.
commonMistakes: Pulling on the head or neck to get up.
Pulling on the neck or head to complete the rep.
Rushing through reps with momentum.
Arching the lower back away from a braced position.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Pulling on the head or neck to get up.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Rest your hands lightly at your temples and lead with your ribs.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Pulling on the neck or head to complete the rep.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Pulling your head does the work your abs should, so your midsection gets less out of it.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your hands light and lead the movement from your midsection.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rushing through reps with momentum.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Momentum does the work your abs should, so the set does less.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Slow each rep down and control both directions.

whyItMatters: The Upright Row builds strength and size in your lateral deltoids, biceps, latissimus dorsi and rear deltoids. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
Set your torso and let your working arm hang with the shoulder blade relaxed forward.
Set a stable base before you begin pulling.
executionSteps: Pull your elbow back toward your hip, leading with the elbow.
Draw the load to your lower ribs and squeeze your shoulder blade back.
Lower under control until your arm is straight and the shoulder blade reaches forward.
coachingTips: Lead with your elbow, not your hand.
Draw the load toward your belt line rather than your chest.
Let your shoulder blade slide back and down at the top of each rep.
Lead with your elbow and feel the side of your shoulder do the work.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
commonMistakes: Yanking with the lower back and using momentum.
Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear while pulling.
Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Yanking with the lower back and using momentum.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Yanking uses your back and momentum instead of the muscles you are rowing with.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your torso still and let your arm and shoulder blade do the work.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear while pulling.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shrugging shoulder takes the pull off your back and into your traps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your shoulder down and pull your elbow straight back.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Skipping the stretch removes the part of the range that builds the most.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Let your arm fully straighten and your shoulder blade reach forward before the next rep.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you pull, breathe in as you return under control.
tempoGuidance: Pull with intent, then lower for about two counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Reach into a full stretch at the bottom and pull until your shoulder blade is fully retracted. Take the lateral deltoids through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Lead with your elbow, not your hand.
Lead with your elbow and feel the side of your shoulder do the work.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
Draw the load toward your belt line rather than your chest.
Let your shoulder blade slide back and down at the top of each rep.
advancedCoachingNotes: Pause and squeeze for one count at the fully retracted position.
beginnerNotes: Use a load you can pull without leaning back or jerking.
equipmentSetup: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
safetyNotes: Reduce the load if you lose control of the movement.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain.
difficultyConsiderations: The Upright Row is a compound dumbbell movement. Each dumbbell is balanced on its own, so both sides have to pull their own weight. Your working limb moves freely, so keep the joint you are training under control. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you balance and control the weight yourself, and it coordinates several joints at once, and it rewards practising the technique.

progressionGuidance.regressionReason: Drop back to Machine Upright Row to groove the movement before you add load or complexity.

whyItMatters: The Waiter Carry builds strength and size in your forearms, trapezius and rectus abdominis. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
Set the joint in a neutral position and keep the rest of your body still.
Pick up the load with a flat back and stand tall.
Set your shoulders back and down before you start walking.
executionSteps: Walk with short, deliberate steps while staying tall.
Keep the load from swinging by holding your sides tight.
Set the load down under control at the end of the distance rather than dropping it.
Move the joint slowly through the largest circle you can control.
coachingTips: Control is the goal — no momentum, and no other joint should move to help.
Stand tall and walk with short, controlled steps.
Keep the load steady rather than letting it swing.
Keep your shoulders back and down for the full distance.
Keep a firm grip and let your forearms do the work.
commonMistakes: Letting the trunk or shoulder swing to make the circle bigger.
Leaning to one side under an uneven load.
Taking long, rushed strides that let the load sway.
Rounding the shoulders forward under the load.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the trunk or shoulder swing to make the circle bigger.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Shrink the circle until only the target joint is moving.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Leaning to one side under an uneven load.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Leaning lets the load win and takes the anti-lean work off your trunk.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Stay stacked and tall, resisting the pull to one side.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Taking long, rushed strides that let the load sway.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A swaying load pulls you around and takes the anti-sway work off your trunk.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Shorten your steps and keep a steady, controlled pace.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rounding the shoulders forward under the load.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Rounded shoulders are a weaker position to carry and hold the load.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your chest up and your shoulders pulled back for the full distance.

breathingGuidance: Breathe steadily and rhythmically throughout the carry.
tempoGuidance: Move at a controlled, deliberate walking pace.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Cover the target distance or time while holding position. Take the forearms and trapezius through their full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Control is the goal — no momentum, and no other joint should move to help.
Stand tall and walk with short, controlled steps.
Keep a firm grip and let your forearms do the work.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
Keep the load steady rather than letting it swing.
advancedCoachingNotes: Increase the distance or load while keeping your torso perfectly upright.
beginnerNotes: Start with a shorter distance and a load you can control the whole way.
equipmentSetup: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
difficultyConsiderations: The Waiter Carry is a dumbbell movement. Each dumbbell is balanced on its own, so both sides have to pull their own weight. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you balance and control the weight yourself.

whyItMatters: The Walking Lunge builds strength and size in your quadriceps, glutes and hamstrings. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
Take a stride long enough that both knees can reach about ninety degrees.
Set your torso tall and your ribs down before the first rep.
executionSteps: Step into the stride and lower straight down rather than forward.
Lower until your back knee is just off the floor.
Drive up through your front foot to return to standing.
coachingTips: Stay tall through your torso — leaning forward turns this into a hinge.
Keep the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Let your knees track in line with your toes.
Push your knees out as you descend into the bottom.
Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.
commonMistakes: Taking a stride so short the front knee travels well past the toes.
Letting the knees cave inward under load.
Rising hips-first so the load shifts forward onto your toes.
Cutting the depth short above parallel.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Taking a stride so short the front knee travels well past the toes.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lengthen the stride until your front shin is close to vertical at the bottom.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the knees cave inward under load.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Caved knees are a weaker position and rob power from the lift.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Push your knees out toward your little toes as you descend and stand.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rising hips-first so the load shifts forward onto your toes.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Hips shooting up first tips you forward and turns the squat into a good morning.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lead with your chest and drive your hips and shoulders up at the same rate.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the depth short above parallel.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shallow squat trains a fraction of the range and much less of your legs.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lower until your hip crease drops below the top of your knee.

breathingGuidance: Take a big breath at the top, hold it through the descent and drive, then exhale at the top.
tempoGuidance: Lower under control for about two counts, then stand with intent.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Aim for thighs at or below parallel while keeping your heels flat on the floor. Take the quadriceps through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Stay tall through your torso — leaning forward turns this into a hinge.
Keep the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
Let your knees track in line with your toes.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add a pause in the bottom position to build strength out of the hole.
beginnerNotes: Start with a box or bench behind you to learn consistent depth.
equipmentSetup: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
difficultyConsiderations: The Walking Lunge is a compound dumbbell movement. Each dumbbell is balanced on its own, so both sides have to pull their own weight. Your hands or feet stay planted, so you move your body against the resistance. It suits newer athletes and is a good place to build the pattern.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Beginner because you balance and control the weight yourself, and it coordinates several joints at once.

progressionGuidance.progressionReason: Move up to Dumbbell Bulgarian Split Squat once you can control this one for all your reps.

whyItMatters: The Z Press builds strength and size in your front deltoids. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
Set your grip just outside shoulder-width with the load at shoulder height.
Squeeze your glutes and take a breath to keep your ribs down.
executionSteps: Press the load straight overhead, moving your head back slightly to clear the path.
Once the load passes your forehead, move your head back through and finish overhead.
Lower under control back to shoulder height.
coachingTips: Finish with the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Squeeze your glutes to stop your lower back from arching.
Keep your forearms vertical throughout the press.
Keep the effort on the front of your shoulders through the press.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to press the load up.
Pressing the load forward instead of straight up.
Stopping short of a full overhead lockout.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Arching the lower back to press the load up.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Arching turns a shoulder press into a decline press and takes tension off your shoulders.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Squeeze your glutes and keep your ribs pulled down.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Pressing the load forward instead of straight up.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A forward press is a weaker, longer path and stresses your shoulders more.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Move your head back to let the load travel in a straight line over your shoulders.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Stopping short of a full overhead lockout.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Without full lockout you miss the top of the press and the strength it builds.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Finish each rep with your elbows locked and the load over your ears.

breathingGuidance: Breathe in and brace at shoulder height, press, then exhale at the top.
tempoGuidance: Press with intent and lower under control for about two counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Lower to shoulder height and press to a full overhead lockout each rep. Take the front deltoids through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Finish with the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Keep the effort on the front of your shoulders through the press.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
Squeeze your glutes to stop your lower back from arching.
Keep your forearms vertical throughout the press.
advancedCoachingNotes: Pause at shoulder height to remove momentum between reps.
beginnerNotes: Use a lighter load and press one arm at a time if bracing is difficult.
equipmentSetup: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
spottingNotes: Use a spotter or set safety pins when the load is heavy on this overhead press, so you can bail a failed rep safely.
safetyNotes: Reduce the load if you lose control of the movement.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain.
difficultyConsiderations: The Z Press is a compound dumbbell movement. Each dumbbell is balanced on its own, so both sides have to pull their own weight. Your working limb moves freely, so keep the joint you are training under control. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you balance and control the weight yourself, and it coordinates several joints at once, and it rewards practising the technique.

whyItMatters: The Zottman Curl builds strength and size in your biceps. As an isolation movement, it targets those muscles directly to build size and balance.
setupInstructions: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
Set a tall torso with your upper arms pinned against your sides.
Start with your arms straight and the load under control.
executionSteps: Bend your elbows and curl the load up while keeping your upper arms still.
Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower under control until your arms are straight.
coachingTips: Keep your elbows pinned to your sides throughout.
Turn your pinky slightly up at the top to finish the squeeze.
Lower all the way until your arm is straight each rep.
Keep the tension on your biceps and stop your elbows from drifting forward.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
commonMistakes: Swinging the torso to start the load moving.
Letting the elbows drift forward to lift the load higher.
Cutting the lower-half of the range short.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Swinging the torso to start the load moving.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A torso swing starts the curl with momentum instead of your biceps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Stand tall and keep your upper arms fixed against your sides.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward to lift the load higher.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Moving the elbows turns a curl into a partial front raise and takes tension off your biceps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your elbows under your shoulders and stop the curl where your upper arm wants to move.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the lower-half of the range short.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Skipping the bottom half leaves strength and size on the table.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Straighten your arm fully at the bottom of each rep.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you curl up, breathe in as you lower.
tempoGuidance: Curl with control and lower for about two counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Move from a fully straight arm to a hard squeeze at the top. Take the biceps through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Keep your elbows pinned to your sides throughout.
Keep the tension on your biceps and stop your elbows from drifting forward.
Control each dumbbell independently so your stronger side doesn’t take over.
Turn your pinky slightly up at the top to finish the squeeze.
Lower all the way until your arm is straight each rep.
advancedCoachingNotes: Slow the lowering phase to three counts to add time under tension.
beginnerNotes: Pick a load you can lift without swinging your body.
equipmentSetup: Choose a pair you can control for every planned rep and get them into position cleanly.
difficultyConsiderations: The Zottman Curl is an isolation dumbbell movement. Each dumbbell is balanced on its own, so both sides have to pull their own weight. Your working limb moves freely, so keep the joint you are training under control. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you balance and control the weight yourself, and it works one joint, so it is simpler to learn.

whyItMatters: The Easy Run builds your aerobic base, work capacity and conditioning.
setupInstructions: Start easy and let the pace settle rather than forcing it.
Set your effort to a pace you can sustain for the planned duration.
Settle into a rhythm before pushing the pace.
executionSteps: Hold a steady, repeatable rhythm for the working duration.
Keep your breathing matched to your pace throughout.
Adjust your effort so the last minute feels as controlled as the first.
Hold a conversational effort for the full duration.
coachingTips: If you could not hold a conversation, you are running this one too hard.
Settle into a cadence you can hold for the full effort.
Breathe rhythmically and in time with your pace.
Build the pace gradually rather than starting too hard.
Run tall with a quick, light cadence and relaxed shoulders and hands.
commonMistakes: Drifting faster as you warm up until the easy run becomes a moderate one.
Starting too fast and fading in the second half.
Tensing the shoulders and upper body while working.
Letting the effort drift down whenever your attention wanders.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Drifting faster as you warm up until the easy run becomes a moderate one.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Check your effort every few minutes and ease back.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Starting too fast and fading in the second half.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A fast start you cannot hold means the back half of the effort suffers.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Open at a pace you could hold to the end, then build.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Tensing the shoulders and upper body while working.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Tension up top wastes energy that should go into your legs and lungs.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Relax your hands, shoulders and face so the effort stays in your legs and lungs.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the effort drift down whenever your attention wanders.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Coasting drops the training effect for that stretch of the effort.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Check your pace regularly and hold it steady to the end.

breathingGuidance: Breathe in a steady rhythm matched to your cadence.
tempoGuidance: Hold a sustainable, repeatable pace for the target duration.
cueHierarchy: If you could not hold a conversation, you are running this one too hard.
Settle into a cadence you can hold for the full effort.
Run tall with a quick, light cadence and relaxed shoulders and hands.
Breathe rhythmically and in time with your pace.
Build the pace gradually rather than starting too hard.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add pace changes or intervals to raise the training stimulus.
beginnerNotes: Use intervals of easier effort to build duration over time.
difficultyConsiderations: The Easy Run is a cardio movement. The machine holds a steady resistance, so settle into a pace you can sustain. It suits newer athletes and is a good place to build the pattern.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Beginner because you can scale the pace and duration to your fitness.

progressionGuidance.progressionReason: Move up to Fartlek Run once you can control this one for all your reps.

whyItMatters: The Explosive Push-Up builds strength and size in your chest, front deltoids and triceps. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Set your hands about shoulder-width, slightly wider than your chest.
Set a straight line from your head to your heels and brace before you begin.
executionSteps: Lower your chest under control toward the floor.
Keep your elbows tucked to about 45 degrees from your torso.
Press back up until your arms are straight.
Move as fast as you can on the way up while staying in control.
coachingTips: Intent is the point — every rep should be maximally fast, and the set ends when speed drops.
Keep a straight line from your head to your heels throughout.
Tuck your elbows to about 45 degrees rather than flaring them wide.
Lower until your chest is just off the floor for a full range.
Think about squeezing your chest to drive the movement, not just pushing with your arms.
commonMistakes: Grinding out slow reps once fatigue sets in.
Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
Only lowering partway before pressing back up.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Grinding out slow reps once fatigue sets in.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: End the set the moment bar or body speed visibly slows.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Sagging hips break the plank line and shift load to your lower back.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Squeeze your glutes and keep a straight line from head to heels.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Flared elbows put your shoulders in a weaker, less comfortable pressing position.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Point your elbows back toward your hips as you lower.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Only lowering partway before pressing back up.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Half reps train a fraction of the range and build less.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lower until your chest is just off the floor each rep.

breathingGuidance: Breathe in as you lower, exhale as you press up.
tempoGuidance: Lower for about two counts, then press up with intent.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Lower until your chest is just off the floor and press to straight arms. Take the chest through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Intent is the point — every rep should be maximally fast, and the set ends when speed drops.
Keep a straight line from your head to your heels throughout.
Think about squeezing your chest to drive the movement, not just pushing with your arms.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
Tuck your elbows to about 45 degrees rather than flaring them wide.
advancedCoachingNotes: Elevate your feet or pause at the bottom to make it harder.
beginnerNotes: Do the movement from your knees or with your hands on a raised surface until you can complete full reps.
difficultyConsiderations: The Explosive Push-Up is a compound bodyweight movement. You move and stabilise your own bodyweight, so change leverage to progress rather than adding weight. Squeeze your glutes and take a breath to keep your ribs down.

Once the load passes your forehead, move your head back through and finish overhead.
Lower under control back to shoulder height.

Squeeze your glutes to stop your lower back from arching.

setupInstructions: Load the sled to a weight you can move steadily and check the surface is clear ahead.
Set the joint in a neutral position and keep the rest of your body still.
Pick up the load with a flat back and stand tall.
Set your shoulders back and down before you start walking.
executionSteps: Walk with short, deliberate steps while staying tall.
Keep the load from swinging by holding your sides tight.
Set the load down under control at the end of the distance rather than dropping it.
Move the joint slowly through the largest circle you can control.

Stand tall and walk with short, controlled steps.

Set a stable, athletic base with your feet under your hips.
Load your hips and take a breath before the explosive rep.
executionSteps: Be explosive on the way up, moving the load or your body as fast as possible.
Absorb the landing or return softly through your hips and knees.
Reset to a stable, balanced position before the next rep.
coachingTips: Be explosive on the way up and controlled on the way down.
Land softly on your mid-foot, absorbing through your hips and knees.
Reset fully between reps rather than rushing the next one.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top of each rep.

whyItMatters: The Sandbag Lunge builds strength and size in your quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings and rectus abdominis. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Load the sled to a weight you can move steadily and check the surface is clear ahead.
Take a stride long enough that both knees can reach about ninety degrees.
Set your torso tall and your ribs down before the first rep.
executionSteps: Step into the stride and lower straight down rather than forward.
Lower until your back knee is just off the floor.
Drive up through your front foot to return to standing.
coachingTips: Stay tall through your torso — leaning forward turns this into a hinge.
Keep the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Let your knees track in line with your toes.
Push your knees out as you descend into the bottom.
Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.
commonMistakes: Taking a stride so short the front knee travels well past the toes.
Letting the knees cave inward under load.
Rising hips-first so the load shifts forward onto your toes.
Cutting the depth short above parallel.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Taking a stride so short the front knee travels well past the toes.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: This takes work off the target muscle and reduces what you get from the set.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lengthen the stride until your front shin is close to vertical at the bottom.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the knees cave inward under load.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Caved knees are a weaker position and rob power from the lift.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Push your knees out toward your little toes as you descend and stand.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rising hips-first so the load shifts forward onto your toes.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Hips shooting up first tips you forward and turns the squat into a good morning.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lead with your chest and drive your hips and shoulders up at the same rate.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the depth short above parallel.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shallow squat trains a fraction of the range and much less of your legs.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lower until your hip crease drops below the top of your knee.

breathingGuidance: Take a big breath at the top, hold it through the descent and drive, then exhale at the top.
tempoGuidance: Lower under control for about two counts, then stand with intent.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Aim for thighs at or below parallel while keeping your heels flat on the floor. Take the quadriceps through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Stay tall through your torso — leaning forward turns this into a hinge.
Keep the load stacked over the middle of your foot.
Drive through your knees and feel the front of your thighs work.
Let your knees track in line with your toes.
Push your knees out as you descend into the bottom.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add a pause in the bottom position to build strength out of the hole.
beginnerNotes: Start with a box or bench behind you to learn consistent depth.
equipmentSetup: Load the sled to a weight you can move steadily and check the surface is clear ahead.
safetyNotes: Reduce the load if you lose control of the movement.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain.

difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you can scale the effort and load to your level, and it coordinates several joints at once, and it demands a high level of skill.

whyItMatters: The Sandbag Over-Shoulder Throw builds strength and size in your upper back, biceps, latissimus dorsi and rear deltoids. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Load the sled to a weight you can move steadily and check the surface is clear ahead.
Set your torso and let your working arm hang with the shoulder blade relaxed forward.
Set a stable base before you begin pulling.
executionSteps: Pull your elbow back toward your hip, leading with the elbow.
Draw the load to your lower ribs and squeeze your shoulder blade back.
Lower under control until your arm is straight and the shoulder blade reaches forward.
coachingTips: Lead with your elbow, not your hand.
Draw the load toward your belt line rather than your chest.
Let your shoulder blade slide back and down at the top of each rep.
Pull with your back and squeeze your shoulder blades together, not just your arms.
commonMistakes: Yanking with the lower back and using momentum.
Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear while pulling.
Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Yanking with the lower back and using momentum.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Yanking uses your back and momentum instead of the muscles you are rowing with.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your torso still and let your arm and shoulder blade do the work.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear while pulling.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shrugging shoulder takes the pull off your back and into your traps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your shoulder down and pull your elbow straight back.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Skipping the stretch removes the part of the range that builds the most.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Let your arm fully straighten and your shoulder blade reach forward before the next rep.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you pull, breathe in as you return under control.
tempoGuidance: Pull with intent, then lower for about two counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Reach into a full stretch at the bottom and pull until your shoulder blade is fully retracted. Take the upper back through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Lead with your elbow, not your hand.
Pull with your back and squeeze your shoulder blades together, not just your arms.
Draw the load toward your belt line rather than your chest.
Let your shoulder blade slide back and down at the top of each rep.
advancedCoachingNotes: Pause and squeeze for one count at the fully retracted position.
beginnerNotes: Use a load you can pull without leaning back or jerking.
equipmentSetup: Load the sled to a weight you can move steadily and check the surface is clear ahead.
safetyNotes: Reduce the load if you lose control of the movement.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain.

difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you can scale the effort and load to your level, and it coordinates several joints at once, and it demands a high level of skill.
